clue.text: Tea bread, say, for ill-disposed Scandinavians

parts.note: the drink tea sounds like the letter T
rolls are an example of bread, hence 'say'

explanation.surface: Someone asks what sort of tea-time loaf would suit unfriendly Nordic folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea' gives its sound-alike letter T; 'say' marks rolls as one example of bread.
explanation.definitionFit: In Norse folklore these are malevolent giants or goblins, hostile creatures of Scandinavian legend.

clue.text: Concerning professional later copy

indicators.note: later tells us the professional piece comes after the first piece in the answer

parts.note: re is a short word meaning about or concerning
pro is short for professional

explanation.surface: A remark about a professional who later produces a copy.
explanation.definitionFit: A reproduction, especially of furniture or art, is a copy made in an older style.

clue.text: Tennyson's showed that slumber was more sweet than toil

definitions.text: Tennyson's showed that slumber was more sweet than toil

parts.words: Tennyson's showed that slumber was more sweet than toil
parts.note: the clue recalls the Choric Song in Tennyson's poem The Lotos-Eaters, where the mariners sing that slumber is sweeter than toil

explanation.surface: A piece of literary criticism about what one of Tennyson's poems argued.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin-Greek name for the lotus-eaters of Homer's Odyssey is the answer; Tennyson's poem gives them the line about slumber.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek name means lotus-eaters, the drugged islanders of the Odyssey whom Tennyson's poem sets singing in praise of rest.

clue.text: Writer of some mettle, they say

indicators.note: they say signals that the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: steel is a metal, and a person of mettle has nerve like steel

explanation.surface: A tribute to an author said to show real courage.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Steele, co-founder of The Tatler and The Spectator, sounds like steel; 'mettle' itself puns on metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Steele was an Irish-born essayist and playwright of the early eighteenth century.

clue.text: Sir John's setter from muggers' haunt

explanation.surface: Falstaff's accomplice turns out to come from a notorious robbers' den.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry IV Part 1 the character Gadshill is called the 'setter', who sets up the robbery for Sir John Falstaff; Gad's Hill in Kent was itself notorious for highwaymen.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the Shakespearean thief who plans the hold-up for Falstaff; the other is the Kent hilltop on the London road where highwaymen robbed travellers.

clue.text: He got the bird in Barnes book

definitions.text: He got the bird in Barnes book

parts.words: He got the bird in Barnes book
parts.note: Julian Barnes's novel Flaubert's Parrot follows the stuffed parrot the French novelist borrowed while writing

explanation.surface: Someone was hissed off, or acquired a parrot, in a novel by Julian Barnes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got the bird' usually means was jeered; here it is literal, the parrot of Barnes's novel Flaubert's Parrot.
explanation.definitionFit: The French author of Madame Bovary is the novelist whose parrot gives Barnes's 1984 book its title.

clue.text: Wilfred Owen's work is rendered powerless

explanation.surface: Owen's poetry is said to have been robbed of its force.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilfred Owen wrote a war poem of this title about a crippled soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Owen's 1917 poem about a maimed young soldier has this title; as an adjective it means incapacitated or put out of action.

clue.text: Philosopher: he holds example supported by student ()

indicators.note: in a down clue, supported by means the student letter sits underneath, after the rest
holds means the first word is put around the abbreviation for example

parts.note: taken as written
e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
L is a learner driver's plate, so a student

explanation.surface: A description of a philosopher who has a pupil propping him up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' wraps HE round EG to give HEGE; 'supported by' puts L below it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was the German idealist thinker behind the dialectic.

clue.text: John Buchan assured us The Moon Endureth. At least for twelve months?

definitions.text: John Buchan assured us The Moon Endureth. At least for twelve months?

parts.words: John Buchan assured us The Moon Endureth. At least for twelve months?
parts.note: Buchan's story collection is titled The Moon Endureth; the clue asks how long the moon lasts, meaning a span of twelve moon cycles

explanation.surface: A wry comment on the title of a John Buchan book, asking whether the moon lasts a year.
explanation.walkthrough: The span described is twelve cycles of the moon, about 354 days.
explanation.definitionFit: This period is twelve synodic months, measured by the moon's phases rather than the sun.

clue.text: Homer's is in the Louvre

parts.note: Ingres painted Homer being crowned among the immortals, and the painting hangs in the Louvre

explanation.surface: A gallery note that something belonging to Homer is on show in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: The painting is Ingres's 1827 canvas of Homer's deification; 'Homer's' looks like a possession but means the elevation of Homer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means deification, elevation to divine status, the subject of Ingres's painting of the poet.

clue.text: Norse peer

parts.note: Ibsen's verse play is named after its hero Peer, a Norwegian

explanation.surface: A Scandinavian nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' looks like a lord but is the first name of Ibsen's hero; the answer is his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibsen's wandering Norwegian hero bears this surname, after Peer.

clue.text: Eponymous ballet girl with rather mechanical reactions

definitions.text: Eponymous ballet girl with rather mechanical reactions

parts.words: Eponymous ballet girl with rather mechanical reactions
parts.note: Delibes's ballet is named after a clockwork doll whom the hero mistakes for a living girl

explanation.surface: A ballerina whose responses on stage seem wooden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rather mechanical' sounds like criticism of a dancer, but the title character is literally an automaton.
explanation.definitionFit: Delibes's 1870 ballet takes its title from the life-size mechanical doll at its centre.

clue.text: James Bridie's diabolus ex machina

parts.note: Bridie's 1943 comedy brings the devil on stage, summoned by a seance, playing on the stage device deus ex machina

explanation.surface: A Scottish playwright's devil who descends to resolve the plot.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridie's play Mr Bolfry has the devil appear in a Highland manse; 'diabolus' replaces 'deus' in the stock phrase for a plot-solving intervention.
explanation.definitionFit: The devil in Bridie's Mr Bolfry is named in the title of the play.

clue.text: Goddess from the other Athenian pantheon

indicators.note: from signals that the letters are taken out of the words that follow, running across them

explanation.surface: A deity drawn from the gods of some rival Greek city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' takes the run of letters straddling 'other Athenian'.
explanation.definitionFit: She is queen of the Olympian deities, wife of Zeus in Greek myth.

clue.text: To Malone I might be excited

indicators.note: might be says the letters could become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tells Malone that they could become agitated with him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' turns the nine letters of TO MALONE I into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being stirred up and full of feeling is the sense of overwrought or worked up.

clue.text: A Christmas carol in chapel? Quite the reverse

definitions.text: A Christmas carol in chapel? Quite the reverse

parts.words: A Christmas carol in chapel? Quite the reverse
parts.note: the name is a chapel in A Christmas Carol, as Scrooge's first name, and a common name for Nonconformist chapels

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a carol is sung in chapel, then reverses the question.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the clue round: not a carol in a chapel but a chapel name in A Christmas Carol, Ebenezer Scrooge; Welsh and Methodist chapels are often called Ebenezer, Hebrew for stone of help.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's miser bears this Hebrew first name, also a frequent title for Nonconformist meeting houses.

clue.text: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well

definitions.text: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well

parts.words: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well
parts.note: Samuel Richardson wrote Pamela and Clarissa wholly as letters exchanged between the characters

explanation.surface: Praise for the novelist Samuel Richardson's handling of his characters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corresponded' looks like 'matched', but means exchanged letters, the device of Richardson's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes writing in letters, the epistolary novel form Richardson made famous.

clue.text: Countless and — orbs / In mazy motion intermingled" (Shelley, Queen Mab)

definitions.text: — orbs / In mazy motion intermingled" (Shelley, Queen Mab)

explanation.surface: A gap in a quotation from Shelley's Queen Mab, beside a one-word definition.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word in Shelley's line 'Countless and unending orbs / In mazy motion intermingled' is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Never finishing, endless, is close to innumerable; it is also the word Shelley used for those orbs.

clue.text: She's been a little —, she's had her head addled by women's talk" (William Dean Howells, Dr Breen's Practice)

definitions.text: She's been a little —, she's had her head addled by women's talk" (William Dean Howells, Dr Breen's Practice)

parts.words: She's been a little —, she's had her head addled by women's talk" (William Dean Howells, Dr Breen's Practice)
parts.note: a quotation from Howells's novel with one word gone; the missing adjective means full of fancies

explanation.surface: A line from a Howells novel with a blank, about a woman whose head has been turned.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap needs an old American sense: fanciful, full of whims and odd ideas.
explanation.definitionFit: In older American usage the word means whimsical or full of fancies, which fits a head addled by talk.

clue.text: Pillbox in main road

indicators.note: in tells us the answer is tucked inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A gun emplacement set up in the middle of a highway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pillbox' suggests a concrete gun post, but it is a box for pills; 'in' takes the run across 'main road'.
explanation.definitionFit: An inro is a small Japanese lacquered case hung from the sash, used to carry medicines.

clue.text: He met a fool in the forest

definitions.text: He met a fool in the forest

parts.words: He met a fool in the forest
parts.note: in As You Like It a melancholy lord says 'A fool, a fool! I met a fool i' the forest', meaning Touchstone in Arden

explanation.surface: A man recounts meeting an idiot among the trees.
explanation.definitionFit: The melancholy courier of Duke Senior in Shakespeare's Arden comedy speaks this line about Touchstone.

clue.text: Browning felt that he was for us, while Shakespeare was of us

definitions.text: Browning felt that he was for us, while Shakespeare was of us

parts.words: Browning felt that he was for us, while Shakespeare was of us
parts.note: Browning's poem The Lost Leader says 'Shakespeare was of us', naming another poet as 'for us'

explanation.surface: A summary of Robert Browning's view of two great English poets.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in The Lost Leader runs 'Shakespeare was of us, Milton was for us'.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning names the author of Paradise Lost as the poet who was 'for us' in The Lost Leader.

clue.text: Hardy offers room for two here…

definitions.text: Hardy offers room for two here…

parts.words: Hardy offers room for two here…
parts.note: Hardy's novel Two on a ... is set on a column used as an observatory, where two lovers meet

explanation.surface: Thomas Hardy is said to provide a spot for a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel is Two on a Tower (1882), where Swithin and Lady Constantine meet at his observatory.
explanation.definitionFit: The tall structure in Hardy's novel title is a monument column fitted as an observatory.

clue.text: Mrs Barclays noxious growth from Java -up a street in Bandung?

definitions.text: Mrs Barclays noxious growth from Java

indicators.note: in signals that the answer lies inside the words given

explanation.surface: Florence Barclay's poisonous plant from Java, which might be found up a street in Bandung.
explanation.walkthrough: Florence Barclay wrote the novel The Upas Tree; the Javanese upas has poisonous sap. 'in' takes the run from 'up a street', and Bandung, a city in Java, keeps the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The upas is a Javanese tree whose sap was used as arrow poison, and also the title of Florence Barclay's novel.

clue.text: … to praise some Tales of Wessex, told by him

indicators.note: some indicates that only part of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: A continuation: Hardy is said to praise his own Wessex tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' takes the run across 'Wessex, told'; the dots link to 22, Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: To laud or glorify someone is to speak highly in their favour.

clue.text: Writer for whom Peter Hgeg's physicist had a feeling?

definitions.text: Writer for whom Peter Hgeg's physicist had a feeling

parts.words: Writer for whom Peter Hgeg's physicist had a feeling
parts.note: Høeg's novel is Smilla's Feeling for ..., whose heroine studies ice; C. P. ... was a British physicist-novelist

explanation.surface: Asks which author a scientist in a Danish novel was fond of.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is C. P. Snow, novelist of the Strangers and Brothers sequence; Høeg's title Smilla's Feeling for Snow gives the 'feeling'.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Snow was a British physicist and novelist, and the Danish novel's title names this kind of weather.

clue.text: One of our characteristics, observed by Haldane

definitions.text: One of our characteristics, observed by Haldane

parts.words: One of our characteristics, observed by Haldane
parts.note: J. B. S. Haldane's essay collection The ... of Man names a trait of humankind

explanation.surface: A trait of humanity noted by the biologist Haldane.
explanation.walkthrough: Haldane's 1932 book is The Inequality of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: Haldane's essays argued that people differ unevenly in ability, the disparity his title names.

clue.text: Okay yet perverse description of Orwell's views?

explanation.surface: A wry remark that Orwell's opinions were fine, or right-wing.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell was a socialist, so calling his views wholly right-wing is perverse; 'yet' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is satisfactory or fine; the other reads the phrase as entirely conservative politically, the opposite of Orwell's left-wing politics.

clue.text: Island featured in a story from Cornwall

definitions.text: Island featured in a story from Cornwall

parts.words: Island featured in a story from Cornwall
parts.note: Barry Cornwall, pen name of Bryan Procter, wrote A ...an Story, named after the Mediterranean island

explanation.surface: An island that appears in a tale set in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cornwall' looks like the English county but is the poet Barry Cornwall, whose poem is A Sicilian Story (1820).
explanation.definitionFit: This Mediterranean island off the toe of Italy gives Barry Cornwall's narrative poem its title.
